idiom_name: Sorbet sealed!/T::Enum + case/when with T.absurd (plain Ruby: case/in + raising else)
implementation_notes: Ruby has no compiler, so the coverage proof has to be imported: with Sorbet a sealed! module (or a T::Enum) fixes the subclass or value set and else T.absurd(x) makes the type checker report every unhandled case, statically and at run time - that is the real replacement for the Visitor structure and the reason the case/when dispatch is load-bearing. Without a type checker, Ruby 3's case/in pattern matching still dispatches on deconstructed variants and raises NoMatchingPatternError when no pattern matches, but completeness is a test-time property, not a proof. Keep classic polymorphic methods or a dispatch table where the class set is open or where the project has no Sorbet/RBS layer.
code_sketch:
class Shape < T::Enum
  enums do
    Circle = new
    Rect   = new
  end
end
def kind(s)
  case s
  when Shape::Circle then :circle
  when Shape::Rect   then :rect
  else T.absurd(s)              # Sorbet: a missing case is a type error
  end
end
pitfalls: T.absurd only fires for cases the checker can see: the argument must be statically typed, and a value that degrades to T.untyped silently disables the proof.
case/when uses Class#===, so ordering matters - a broad class listed first swallows later variants and the checker may then report the other arms as unreachable.
Sorbet sealing is file-scoped: a sealed! module requires every subclass to be declared in the same file, which concentrates the whole variant set in one place and makes it a merge hotspot.
Without Sorbet or RBS, a missing arm raises NoMatchingPatternError only on the code paths that actually execute - production traffic becomes the test suite.
